analysis.one_liner: Ends the federal tax deduction employers get for anti-union campaigns aimed at their own workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 28 senators, never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies can currently deduct the cost of consultants, meetings, and campaigns designed to persuade employees against unionizing — meaning taxpayers effectively subsidize those campaigns. The bill would deny that deduction, require employers to report such spending to the IRS each quarter, and make expenses tied to any unfair labor practice charge non-deductible. It also carves out exceptions for direct bargaining with a union, shareholder communications, and voluntarily recognizing a union.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers deciding whether to form or join a union, because employer campaigns to influence those decisions would no longer be partly paid for by taxpayers. Union members and workers in labor disputes also benefit, since employer spending on elections, disputes, and collective actions would lose its tax advantage.

how_it_helps.text: Employers currently deduct the cost of anti-union consultants and campaigns as ordinary business expenses, shifting part of the cost to taxpayers; the bill ends that subsidy for spending meant to influence employees about labor organizations, elections, disputes, and collective actions.

Employers would have to report to the IRS, at least annually, the dates, amounts, and nature of any attempt to influence employees about labor organizations, creating a public paper trail that does not exist today.

Expenses tied to an unfair labor practice complaint, settlement, or a federal finding of interference or coercion would become non-deductible, so employers charged with violating labor law could no longer write off the campaigns that led to the charge.

The bill's findings cite Economic Policy Institute research that employers were charged with unfair labor practices in roughly 4 of 10 union elections in 2016-2017 and that companies spent $340 million yearly on outside consultants to sway workers' views.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that spend money influencing employees about unions would pay more in taxes by losing the deduction, and the union-avoidance consulting industry would likely see demand fall. Taxpayers would stop picking up part of the cost of these campaigns.

drawbacks.text: The deduction denial reaches broadly: it covers wages and time spent in any meeting or training where labor organizations are discussed, which employers could argue sweeps in ordinary workplace communications and imposes compliance costs and tax uncertainty beyond true 'union busting' campaigns.

Linking tax treatment to pending unfair labor practice charges means an employer's tax bill turns on a National Labor Relations Board complaint before any final decision, which critics of the NLRB could call a penalty without due process.

It is a one-sided tax tool: unions' own persuasion spending was never deductible in the same way, but the bill does nothing to change other employer advantages in union elections, so it raises the cost of one tactic without changing the underlying election rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the upside is real but indirect: ending a taxpayer subsidy makes anti-union campaigns more expensive without banning them, and the new reporting would expose how much employers spend to influence organizing decisions. The main costs fall on employers and consultants, though the bill's wide definition of covered meetings could create tax and compliance questions for routine workplace discussions. On balance it is a modest, well-aimed change whose loss means the status quo — employer influence campaigns partly paid for by taxpayers — continues.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or vote there, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Casey introduced the bill on May 12, 2022, with 19 original cosponsors including Sen. Wyden, the chair of the Finance Committee to which it would go.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that run anti-union campaigns keep a tax deduction for the cost, and the union-avoidance consulting industry keeps its market; workers deciding whether to organize got no change.

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to end the tax deduction for employer anti-union campaigns and recruited 19 original cosponsors.

for.name: 28 senators
for.role: 27 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate Independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sen. Wyden, who chaired the Finance Committee where it was referred.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a bill cosponsor
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 28 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independents; no Senate Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would strip a tax deduction from spending on campaigns to influence employees about unions — an outside-consultant market the bill's findings put at $340 million a year. Its interest in the bill ran against workers' organizing decisions.

Employer campaigns would become more expensive and would have to be reported to the IRS, making it costlier for employers to sway workers against organizing. Unions are not an industry, but they are the concentrated beneficiary on the other side.
